‘Collapsing confidence’ in housing market, Wilson says

Tim Wilson has jumped on that reporting around rent increases and says there has been a collapse in confidence since the budget which is hurting renters.

We’ve had, since the budget, collapsing confidence, a lack of will to invest in housing that is going to be available for rentals.

We’re seeing a complete disaster in the housing market, and we know that’s only going to do one thing while the government continues to overshoot its migration target, and that is an increase in rents on Australians struggling to save a first home deposit.

There is an awful lot that goes into determining rents in Australia, and the thing that Treasury modelled in the context of the budget, what is the isolated effect of what the government actually changed about the housing market. And if I just step back for a second, we’ve got a broken housing system in our country, and it’s the renters of Australia who are bearing the brunt of really 40 years of government’s not doing enough about this problem.

I think that Clare sadly needs to start taking a bit of responsibility for her housing policy. But also, Clare, stop gaslighting Australians, stop gaslighting the mum and dads who are currently watching this show and feeling the impact of your toxic housing taxes … She can sit on your show and defend her policies, but the evidence on the ground, the evidence from the experts, is that Labor’s toxic housing taxes are smashing the market.

The wild capture and release of a female big cat into a nature reserve is the first step towards reintroducing a population that hasn’t been seen for 70 years

On 31 July, “Umit” – which means hope in Kazakh – was released into a nature reserve on the edge of Lake Balkhash after more than a decade of careful planning to return the caspian tiger to the region. With this release, Kazakhstan became the first country to restore its tiger range after they had been thought extinct, with the last reliable sighting in the country recorded more than 70 years ago.

Umit – a wild-caught female tiger transported from the Russian far east – will be joined by more big cats in the coming years, with plans to establish a self-sustaining population of about 50. A wild-caught male flown from Russia is still being monitored by authorities and will be released when he is judged fit to survive alone. Two wild tiger cubs are also being reared on the reserve in special enclosures, with as little human contact as possible, and are likely to be released into the marshlands next year, to feast on boar, deer and kulans, a type of wild donkey.

items.content_html: Pressure is mounting on the FIFA president Gianni Infantino after plans to sell a stake in the World Cup collapsed and fresh allegations emerged relating to his time at UEFA.

items.title: Germany: Interior Minister warns of 'daily' hybrid warfare
items.content_html: German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt says attacks by foreign powers have become a constant threat to Germany. His remarks come just days after an explosive-laden drone was found at Leipzig airport.

items.title: When German Catholics and Protestants share a church
items.content_html: Each year, dozens of churches are decommissioned, demolished or repurposed in Germany. But there is a new, unique development.

items.title: Germany debates reintroducing mandatory civilian service
items.content_html: Social organizations are skeptical about the government's ideas for a civilian service program that youths could choose as an alternative should Germany reinstate mandatory military conscription.

items.title: Eco wins: Hungary goes solar, marmots go viral and Rome gets an upgrade
items.content_html: From Hungary's accidental solar revolution to marmot crowdfunding and a long-overdue upgrade for Rome's big snake, good news comes in strange packages this week.

items.title: Germany: Far-right AfD extends its lead in nationwide polls
items.content_html: In the latest Sunday poll, the AfD continues to pull ahead. And more and more people are against excluding the right-wing populists from decision-making, at least on a case-by-case basis.

items.title: Testosterone and fertility: the trade-off men aren't told about
items.content_html: Testosterone is trending in gyms, on social online and in politics. US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth even wants troops screened for low testosterone. But taking supplements can shut down the body's natural production.

items.title: Drought threatens power supplies in Danube countries
items.content_html: Droughts, heat and falling water levels in the Danube are hitting central and southeastern Europe hard. Hungary and Romania are experiencing an energy crisis — whereas countries like Bulgaria are better prepared.

items.title: Mata Hari: Celebrated dancer turns WWI spy
items.content_html: Mata Hari enthralled Europe's elite with her beauty and performances. Accused of spying during World War I, she faced a French firing squad in 1917.

items.title: AfD threatens to cut funding for 'modern-thinking' culture
items.content_html: The far-right party could win an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt's state election in September. Their cultural program denigrates Bauhaus, Holocaust remembrance culture and diversity in theater.

items.title: How Gianni Infantino rose to rule football
items.content_html: Gianni Infantino is staying on as FIFA president despite growing pressure to step down. So who is football's most powerful man, why did UEFA and others turn against him, and how did he reassert his authority?

items.title: Why is Russia selling its gold?
items.content_html: Russia has become one of the world's biggest sellers of gold over the past 12 months. It's an attempt to raise cash in the face of budget issues, but not necessarily a sign of a looming financial crisis.

items.title: The hidden problem with small modular nuclear reactors
items.content_html: Mini nuclear reactors are seen as a flexible energy source. Their promise: abundant energy, cheap, clean and climate-friendly with lower water use. But do the numbers add up? We look at what's behind the SMR hype.

items.title: My sleep deprivation is your natural short sleep
items.content_html: Every so often we hear of high-ranking politicians or CEOs claiming to get by on very little sleep — some as little as three hours a night. If they're not natural short sleepers, chances are they're heading for trouble.

items.title: AI ecosystem's 'circular' investment: risk or advantage?
items.content_html: Amid talk of an AI sector bubble, one aspect is under scrutiny. Many big AI players are invested in smaller ones, who then buy the bigger firm's products. This brings risks and advantages.

items.title: South Sudan: How climate change can result in toxic water
items.content_html: Years of flooding have resulted in disastrous water pollution in South Sudan's main oil region. As communities, scientists and health workers scramble for solutions, the long-term impacts of the crisis is yet to emerge.

items.title: Tennis star Sabalenka supports sport's new sex test policy
items.content_html: The world number one women's tennis player supports the WTA's new sex testing rules. Others are more critical of the policy.

items.title: More cancer-prone? Why younger generations may be at risk
items.content_html: Researchers are observing certain age-related types of cancer more frequently in younger people. A new study suggests this could be because younger generations are aging faster than their parents or grandparents.

items.title: Binging on cringe: It's as addictive as 'eating junk food'
items.content_html: Flexing achievements? Cringe. Expressing genuine emotions? Cringe. You want to look away, but you can’t. Cringe. It's so addictive, people have built social media careers by monetizing other people's worst moments.

items.title: What happens next for Infantino and FIFA?
items.content_html: FIFA President Gianni Infantino is under pressure after the failure of his plan to create a commercial subsidiary for the World Cup. But will he be ousted? And what is needed for that to happen?

items.title: The economic toll of Spain's wildfires
items.content_html: Devastating wildfires are ravaging Spain's tourism, economy and nature. Could the country have done more to prevent them?

items.title: Germany: As temperatures rise, so does climate skepticism
items.content_html: Some 98% of active climate scientists say climate change is happening, and is man-made. Nonetheless, a new study shows the number of climate-change skeptics in Germany has increased. Why is that?

items.title: More women die in heatwaves, but biology 'isn't main cause'
items.content_html: In country after country, more women are dying from the heat than men. But researchers say biology isn't the main reason. Age, working conditions, and unequal access to rest may drive the gap.

items.title: What's really causing Europe's wildfires
items.content_html: From Greece to France, Europe is burning. But what's the real reason for the historic blazes ripping through the continent and why are they getting harder to stop?

items.title: From petitions to memes: How students made dissent visible
items.content_html: From imperial China to present-day India, student movements have repeatedly adapted the tools and symbols of their age to challenge authority.

items.title: Humanoid robots: Trump's latest China trade battle?
items.content_html: The US has banned foreign-made humanoid robots, a market Chinese tech firms dominate. Although Washington cited national security risks, analysts think Donald Trump is buying time for US robot makers to catch up.

items.title: Eco wins: From death strip to nature haven and other green surprises
items.content_html: A Cold War relic becomes a biodiversity haven, a Pokemon Go for trees and seagrass gets a second life. This week's eco wins come from some unexpected places.

items.title: FIFA plans: Infantino under pressure as senior advisor quits
items.content_html: After regional football federations condemned FIFA plans for private investment, Carlos Cordeiro, senior advisor to FIFA President Gianni Infantino, tendered his resignation.

items.title: German court rules that AI music firm Suno violated copyrights
items.content_html: Germany's state-mandated licensing agency, GEMA, says the verdict has "global significance," as Suno is also directed to pay yet-to-be-quantified damages.

items.title: BMW to Volkswagen: How deep is Germany's auto industry cull?
items.content_html: BMW joins VW, Porsche and Mercedes-Benz in cutting thousands of jobs, as Chinese rivals erode their market share. DW recaps the major reforms German automakers are pursuing to safeguard their future.

items.title: Why Germany may stand up against FIFA's World Cup sell-off
items.content_html: Leading figures in German football have lined up to criticize Gianni Infantino’s plans to sell a stake in the World Cup. Germany is showing signs that they may be ready to oppose Infantino's re-election.

items.title: 'Rienzi': Why this Wagner opera is so relevant today
items.content_html: The opera sparked controversy long before its Bayreuth Festival premiere, and the debate hasn't died down since it came to the stage. Now, another controversy surrounds the new AI-generated Ring cycle.

items.title: K-pop's BTS opt out of new Asian music Grammy consideration
items.content_html: The K-pop sensation BTS, snubbed when nominated for Grammys in the past, say they're not interested in winning a new Asian music category.

items.title: World Cup sell-off: Has FIFA finally gone too far?
items.content_html: A new FIFA proposal to sell off a stake in the World Cup has been met with fury in the football world. Under Gianni Infantino’s presidency, FIFA has become increasingly profit-driven, but is this too much?

items.title: Bayreuth Festival opens with celebration and commemoration
items.content_html: To mark its 150th anniversary, the Bayreuth Festival remembers victims of the Holocaust — and confronts its founder's antisemitism.

items.title: How two wars and El Nino could fuel world hunger
items.content_html: The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East haven't yet crippled global food supplies. Add a powerful weather pattern like El Nino, however, and the risks multiply.

items.title: Germany: How weather extremes impact local agriculture
items.content_html: Heat, drought, heavy rain and late frosts are taking a toll on German farmers. They increasingly respond with adapted varieties, new crops, modern breeding techniques and modified farming methods.

items.title: FIFA plans to form new commercial subsidiary and sell stake
items.content_html: FIFA has announced plans to form a commercial subsidiary and to sell a non-controlling interest to private investors. It needs approval from member associations, but is claiming that it will benefit them financially.

items.title: Why is Germany building roads for yesterday's climate?
items.content_html: As the Autobahn buckles under heat waves, Germany is still paving roads for a past climate. Engineers know how to fix that — so what's the holdup?

items.title: 'Loneliness influencers': Being alone brings in the clicks
items.content_html: No friends, no dating, no problem? Many influencers are presenting social isolation as a lifestyle. But experts warn of the consequences.

items.title: Bernadette Amani 'living her dream' at Bayern and WAFCON
items.content_html: Bernadette Amani joined Bayern Munich in January and is now captaining Ivory Coast in their first WAFCON in 12 years. Getting to the top hasn't been a straight path for the newly crowned German double winner.

items.title: As US-Iran war rages, who's risking the Strait of Hormuz?
items.content_html: Though Iran continues to attack vessels as leverage in its war with the United States, data show that several shippers continue to transit the waterway.

items.title: 'Amnesia' about measles risk and low vaccination rates have helped US infections grow
items.content_html: The latest US data show measles cases from January to mid-July 2026 totaled more than all cases in 2025. Experts blame a fall in vaccination and warn that people have forgotten measles can be life-threatening.

items.title: FIFA boss Infantino takes aim at World Cup critics
items.content_html: In a strongly worded open statement, FIFA President Gianni Infantino has hit out at those he says were too "consumed by hate and criticism" to enjoy the tournament. Infantino brushed off a number of corruption concerns.

items.title: Car ramming attacks: Why do they keep happening?
items.content_html: Cars are being used as weapons, to ram, kill and maim innocent people. The reasons why are not always clear, nor are solutions to preventing such attacks.

items.title: WAFCON 2026: What you need to know
items.content_html: Several months after it was supposed to start and with more teams than first planned, WAFCON 2026 is finally set to begin. The hosts want a maiden title while a tournament outsider have one of its best players.

items.title: Lenacapavir will slow HIV infections if there's enough of it and it reaches at-risk groups
items.content_html: Lenacapavir is one injection, twice a year. It's a big improvement for people in high-risk groups, currently taking a pill a day against HIV infection. But its long-term impact depends on it reaching those very people.

items.title: Tour de France final stage shortened due to wildfires
items.content_html: Security personnel assigned to the race have been redeployed to help contain major blazes near Bordeaux, reducing Sunday's final stage.

items.title: Eco wins: Cities, creatures, and tech are saving the day
items.content_html: From an AI-powered cute little pangolin, heat mapping to cool down cities and animals reducing wildfire risks by doing their thing, these real-world climate hacks are helping communities stay ahead of a changing planet.

items.title: Highs and lows as Bayreuth Festival turns 150
items.content_html: The Bayreuth Festival's 150th anniversary has been clouded by controversy surrounding German-Jewish speaker Michel Friedman. Yet it offers an opportunity to celebrate, including with an AI-enhanced Ring cycle.

items.title: Why Trump's 'forced labor' tariffs leave the world puzzled
items.content_html: After the US Supreme Court struck down Donald Trump's emergency tariffs, the White House has turned to another trade law linked to alleged human rights abuses.

items.title: The trees helping fires spread and what to do about it‌
items.content_html: With Spain declaring an emergency, France seeking EU help and Canada dealing with more than 900 hot spots, wildfires are out of control. Monocultures and climate change are partly to blame but can we stop the burning?

items.title: How vanilla's history is not so … 'vanilla'
items.content_html: Long before "vanilla" meant bland, the bean's fandom spanned Mesoamerican elites to European courts. But it owes its ubiquity to a 12-year-old enslaved boy.

items.title: Klopp named new head coach of Germany men's football team
items.content_html: Germany has turned to Jürgen Klopp to lead a new era for the four-time world champions after their disappointing World Cup exit, with hopes of building toward future international tournaments.

items.title: Jürgen Klopp and Germany: A partnership long in the making
items.content_html: In one of the worst-kept secrets in football, the former Dortmund and Liverpool boss has been named head coach of the German men's national team.

items.title: Spain's solar eclipse trilogy: Spectacle starts August 12
items.content_html: From August 2026 to January 2028, amateur and pro sky watchers are in for a series of rare solar spectacles over Spain and North Africa. Astronomers expect the events to attract millions from around the world.

items.title: ECB keeps interest rates unchanged amid Iran war inflation
items.content_html: The European Central Bank has kept its base interest rates steady but said it was "closely monitoring" the energy price shock. The impact of the war against Iran on energy costs has pushed inflation over ECB targets.

items.title: Oil prices jump as Hormuz, Red Sea crises deepen
items.content_html: Renewed strikes on shipping in the Gulf and the Red Sea have dealt a fresh double blow to global oil markets, with the price of crude oil once again passing $100 a barrel. DW examines what could push prices even higher.

items.title: US citizens are ramping up pressure on data centers
items.content_html: Rapid data center construction across the US, fueled by AI, comes with serious threats to the environment, public health and energy supply. Local opposition has blocked or delayed dozens of projects.

items.title: US-China AI rivalry heats up as Chinese models gain ground
items.content_html: China's AI platforms are rapidly closing the gap with their US counterparts, prompting fresh threats from the Trump administration. With accusations of intellectual property theft, could tensions boil over?

items.title: Female coaches want more representation in African football
items.content_html: Female head coaches will be a rare sight at the Women’s African Cup of Nations. However, there are some promising signs.

items.title: Will surge in German business bankruptcies hit growth?
items.content_html: Company insolvencies in Germany are rising sharply. Is this a sign of deeper economic weakness, or just a market correction that could ultimately benefit future growth?

items.title: Austria turns Hitler's birthplace into police station
items.content_html: The house where Adolf Hitler was born in 1889 is now a police station. Austrian authorities have long sought to prevent it becoming a neo-Nazi pilgrimage site.

items.title: Can VR help you achieve your goals?
items.content_html: A Max Planck researcher has developed VR and smartphone tools that let you "meet" your future self. The science behind it is more powerful than it sounds.

items.title: 'Antifa' song climbs to top of charts after TV show cancellation
items.content_html: German rapper Danger Dan and pianist Igor Levit had been invited to play a song for the 100th episode of a political satire show on TV. The performance was canceled at the last minute due to its message.

items.title: Why the youth jobs crisis is becoming global
items.content_html: Young people in much of the world face growing competition for entry-level jobs as graduate numbers rise, hiring slows and AI-driven disruption adds uncertainty to career prospects.

items.title: How heat waves are messing with your sleep
items.content_html: Residents across Europe have struggled to sleep during the latest record heat waves. But as the planet continues to warm, sleep deprivation could create an epidemic of mental and physical ill-health.
